title: service-perimeter-split-controlplane-dataplane-notes
content:
Context: customer wants a POC that demonstrates private inference for a regulated workload. Requirements: no public ingress to model-serving nodes, auditable control-plane commands, optional customer-managed KMS, predictable egress path for external downloads/updates, and ability to roll back to a hosted fallback. This doc sketches a proposal for splitting the service perimeter (control plane vs data plane), DNS/delegation approaches, ingress/egress patterns, endpoint choices, and a test checklist for the POC.

Goals and constraints:
- Control plane must be able to push model versions, manage rollouts, and receive health/usage telemetry. Customer prefers control-plane metadata to be visible in their audit logs (optionally hosted in their account).
- Data plane (model-serving GPUs) must only accept requests from customer networks or a tightly-controlled ingress (no public IPs).
- Minimal changes to customer infra: prefer VPC attachment + interface endpoints over heavy network redesign.
- Preserve source IP when possible for downstream auth (some customers use IP-based allowlists).
- Work within corporate security constraints: mTLS, mutual auth, and KMS integration.

Proposal summary (3 options):
1) Hosted control plane + private reverse tunnel (fast MVP)
   - Overview: Redwood-hosted control plane communicates to customer data plane via persistent outbound mTLS reverse tunnels from the data-plane subnet to Redwood control-plane endpoints. No control-plane ingress into customer VPC.
   - DNS: internal data-plane resolves control-plane by Redwood-managed private hostname over the tunnel; no conditional forwarder required.
   - Egress: data-plane egress uses customer NAT for external downloads; control-plane traffic goes over tunnel.
   - Pros: minimal customer network change, fast to stand up for POC.
   - Cons: customers with strict outbound-only policies may block, audit trail for control-plane events not in customer logs unless forwarded.

2) Customer-hosted control plane (higher-compliance)
   - Overview: Deploy control-plane components into a customer shared-services VPC (or private deployment package). Redwood provides AMIs/containers; control-plane runs under customer's account. Control plane talks to Redwood only for software updates & telemetry through a configurable egress proxy.
   - DNS: control-plane has private hosted zone owned by customer for all control-plane FQDNs; data-plane resolves using private resolution.
   - Egress: all outbound to Redwood (for metrics/agent updates) goes via interface endpoints or customer-managed proxy with TLS inspection configured per agreement.
   - Pros: audit logs remain in customer account, full control over KMS and IAM.
   - Cons: longer setup, maintenance burden for customer; version sync requires careful rollout.

3) Hybrid (control plane in customer shared VPC + Redwood-managed ops plane)
   - Overview: Control plane runs in customer account but Redwood provides a small managed ops plane (for emergency fallbacks and telemetry ingestion). Traffic is limited, authenticated, and whitelisted.
   - DNS: split-horizon with conditional forwarders to Redwood ops endpoints for limited domains.
   - Pros/Cons: balances visibility with operational support.

DNS and resolution patterns (detailed):
- Recommendation: use a customer-owned private hosted zone (Route53 or equivalent) with delegation for control-plane hostnames. Provide Terraform module to create records: cp-api.customer.internal -> ENI/interface endpoint private IP or internal ALB depending on pattern.
- Conditional forwarders on customer DNS servers if they have on-prem DCs that need to resolve Redwood test harness hosts.
- Avoid exposing wildcard public records. If cross-account lookup is required, prefer VPC peering + shared hosted zone rather than public records.
- For mTLS bootstrap, provide short-lived SRV/TXT tokens published in the private hosted zone with strict TTL and retrieval via authenticated ephemeral instance profile.

Ingress patterns to data plane (no public IPs requirement):
- Interface endpoint-based ingress (recommended for AWS): set up an internal NLB in customer's shared-services VPC with security groups that restrict to specific CIDR blocks. Data-plane instances subscribe to this NLB via private routing.
- Optional sidecar reverse-proxy in customer infra (e.g., envoy) that terminates TLS and forwards to model-serving nodes over mTLS with identity pins.
- If source IP preservation is required: do not use NAT at the last hop — use TLS termination in the same VPC and avoid proxy that SNATs. Document how ALB/NLB preserve client IPs and configure target group type accordingly.

Egress and dependency management:
- Prefer customer-managed S3/registry VPC endpoints (gateway or interface). Provide a manifest of required external endpoints (hashes, package URLs) so customer can pre-approve and create VPC endpoints.
- For OS/agent updates where outbound to the internet is unavoidable, provide an option to stage artifacts into a customer S3 bucket and retrieve over S3 endpoint — removes need for open egress.
- If a centralized outbound proxy is required for traffic inspection, provide support for proxy auth and health-checks, and document circuit-breaker behavior so model-serving nodes degrade gracefully if egress is blocked.

Endpoint choices matrix (quick):
- KMS: interface endpoint (customer-managed KMS in account) — recommended for key ownership.
- S3: gateway endpoint for performance/cost efficiency.
- STS/IAM: interface endpoints to avoid public calls.
- Container registry: interface endpoint or registry mirror in customer account (recommended for air-gapped).

Observability and rollout hooks:
- Metrics/telemetry: push metrics to local metrics collector (Prometheus pushgateway or StatsD) and forward to Redwood observability only if customer consents.
- Canary: use tag-based routing in control plane to roll out new model weights to a small subset of instances using placement tags and canary profiles.
- Tracing: instrument sproc to add trace-ids and ensure sampling is configurable by customer.

Test checklist for POC (actionable items):
- Network: validate route table entries from shared-services -> data-plane and back. Test routing with socat/curl.
- DNS: resolve cp-api FQDN from an instance in data-plane VPC and verify response and TLS certificate common name.
- mTLS: perform mutual TLS handshake test using test-client certs (we provide minimal test client).
- Egress: simulate blocked internet egress and confirm model-serving uses staged S3 for downloads; verify graceful failure metrics.
- Source IP: issue request through NLB and confirm target sees original client IP (iptables or application logs).
- KMS: encrypt/decrypt sample blob with customer KMS key from a data-plane node across the chosen endpoint.
- Failover: shut down primary control-plane (if hosted) and verify fallback to emergency ops plane or local cached model.

Risks and mitigation:
- Customer firewall blocks outbound tunnels: prepare plan B (customer-hosted control plane or explicit firewall allow lists).
- Token leakage in DNS TXT records: use ephemeral tokens with short TTL and rotate during handshake.
- Version drift between customer control plane and Redwood's release: schedule sync windows and automated compatibility checks.

Open questions for customer workshop:
- Can we run a customer-hosted control plane in their shared-services VPC for the POC?
- Do they require source IP preservation for downstream policy enforcement?
- Are there on-prem DNS resolvers that must be able to resolve control-plane FQDNs?
- KMS policy: who should own CMKs for model encryption?

Next steps (owner assignments):
- Aisha: prepare Terraform module for private hosted zone + interface endpoint blueprint (ETA: 2 weeks).
- Tomás: integration tests for mTLS reverse-tunnel + cert rotation (ETA: 1 week).
- Claire: draft customer-facing one-pager with diagram and choices (ETA: 1 week).
- Jamal: setup POC test harness repo and initial Terratest cases (ETA: 2 weeks).

Notes to self: keep POC scope narrow: start with Hosted-control-plane + reverse tunnel to prove model serving without public ingress. Only expand to customer-hosted control plane if compliance gate requires it. Capture all decisions in Confluence link in linked_artifacts and append network diagrams (PNG) to that page.

References and templates included in linked_artifacts above.

End of notes.
